q: Lecture 4 – Orbit – slide 5: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
The exophthalmometer is placed on the lowest point of the temporal zygomatic.

  • To avoid parallactic measurement errors, the examiner moves his own eye horizontally until the two integral graduations (black right arrowheads) align in the projection (black left arrow).
  • Once the graduations are aligned, the examiner reads the value of the extraorbital prominence of the anterior surface of the cornea (long white arrow) on the scale (short white arrows).
  • The examiner reads the measurement with only one eye.
  • left eye to read the value for the patient’s right eye and vice versa.

q: Lecture 4 – Orbit – slide 12: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Typical signs

  • exophthalmos, (readily apparent in the left eye)
  • retraction of the upper eyelid with visible sclera superior to the limbus (Dalrymple’s sign),
  • conjunctival injection, and fixed gaze (Kocher’s sign).

q: Lecture 4 – Orbit – slide 25: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Orbital celulitis

  • exophthalmos
  • severe chemosis (conjunctival swelling)
  • eyelid swelling,
  • Significantly limited ocular motility (“cemented” globe)
  • Patients may exhibit
  • leukocytosis
  • increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
  • Where there is clinical evidence of involvement of the paranasal sinuses, an ENT specialist should be consulted to evaluate the sinuses and initiate any necessary treatment.
